Summary for Your ManuscriptWhen writing this up, this pattern allows you to argue that the cell’s metabolic adaptation is controlled by distinct, independent regulatory modules.Instead of a messy, continuous slide where metabolic pathways gradually drift across multiple profiles, the transition behaves like an electronic circuit board: specific, clean metabolic pathways are systematically switched "ON" and "OFF" in tight synchronization with your early ($06\text{h}$) versus late ($24\text{h}$) phenotypic waves.

1. What Drives Row Re-Ordering (y-axis)

Because each cluster has its own distinct set of rows, the vertical sorting is determined by how cleanly concentrated the signal is, and which specific columns it aligns with.

    Perfect Synchrony Aggregation: If five different rows are all highly significant in Cluster 3 and completely zero everywhere else, their mathematical distance from each other is 0. The algorithm instantly snaps them together into a tight vertical block.

    Proximity to Neighboring Profiles: Even though the active blocks don't overlap, the algorithm has to stack them sequentially from top to bottom. It looks at the overall similarity of the entire row profile. If Cluster A and Cluster B are horizontally placed next to each other by the column sorter, the rows unique to Cluster A will be positioned right next to the rows unique to Cluster B. This creates the clean, sweeping diagonal "staircase" effect typical of perfectly partitioned data.

2. What Drives Column Re-Ordering (x-axis)

This is where the most interesting math happens. Since the clusters don't share any active rows, how does R know which column should go first, second, or third? It uses the magnitude of the background baseline and overall distance.

When calculating Euclidean distance between two columns (C1​ and C2​) with non-overlapping active rows, the formula simplifies dramatically. The distance is driven by the absolute sums of their enrichment strengths:
Distance=∑(Active Signals in C1​)2+∑(Active Signals in C2​)2​

The column re-ordering is therefore driven by:

    Signal Volume and Density: Clusters that have a similar total amount of enrichment weight (e.g., both contain a few highly significant pathways vs. both containing many weakly significant pathways) will have shorter mathematical distances between them. The algorithm groups columns with similar overall "functional impact" or signal scales closer together.

    The Shape of the Zeroes: The distance matrix penalizes columns that have massive, towering spikes next to columns that are completely flat. Therefore, columns with lower, quieter active signals naturally group on one side of the heatmap, while highly volatile clusters with massive enrichment weights push to the other side.

In Short:

Because your data is perfectly modular, the algorithm isn't sorting by "shared functions." Instead, it is sorting by coordination and magnitude. It automatically arranges the x-axis so that clusters with similar total response intensities sit side-by-side, and then it effortlessly lines up the y-axis rows to mirror that exact horizontal sequence, turning a non-sequential scatterplot into a beautifully organized diagonal timeline.

This output gives you a clear look at the cell's metabolic priorities. Instead of a general, across-the-board stress response, your high-level map has isolated a specific, coordinated chemical defense and metabolic recycling hub.

Here is how these four precise terms fit together biologically, followed by the specific search terms we can use to see if the rest of this network is active.
1. Biological Interpretation: The Multi-Step Detox Sieve

When these four terms light up together in the same cluster wave, they tell a cohesive story about how the cell handles toxic intermediates and shifts its energy strategy:

    Monooxygenase Activity (The Initial Strike): This is your phase-1 defense. Monooxygenases use molecular oxygen to break open tough chemical rings (like phenylacetic acid or aromatic hydrocarbons) or append hydroxyl groups to foreign molecules. This makes a hydrophobic toxin soluble so the cell can actually degrade it.

    Cellular Detoxification of Aldehyde (Cleaning Up the Mess): Breaking down aromatics and hydrocarbons invariably creates aldehydes as highly reactive, toxic intermediates. If aldehydes build up, they cross-link proteins and destroy the cell. Seeing this term in the exact same cluster means the cell isn't just chopping up the primary toxin; it has synchronized its phase-2 defenses to neutralize the dangerous byproducts of that breakdown instantly.

    Detoxification of Nitrogen Compounds (Managing the Waste): As the cell modifies these compounds or shifts its amino acid pools to deal with the stress, it generates excess nitrogen waste (like ammonia). This term indicates the presence of an active metabolic exit-valve processing that nitrogen load to prevent internal toxicity.

    Glycine Decarboxylation via Glycine Cleavage System (The Energy Shift): This is the bridge to central metabolism. The glycine cleavage system is a massive multienzyme complex. When it breaks down glycine, it feeds 1-carbon units directly into the folate pool and generates NADH.

    This tells you that the cell is likely under energy stress from driving the energy-expensive monooxygenase defenses. It is aggressively scavenging glycine to harvest high-energy electrons (NADH) and power its survival machinery.

```{r}
# ==============================================================================
# FACETED DETOXIFICATION & METABOLIC SHUNT INFRASTRUCTURE
# ==============================================================================
message("Compiling expanded, 4-panel faceted detoxification heatmap...")

# 1. EXPANDED SEARCH & CORE HEURISTIC ROUTING
fig6_faceted_data <- compiled_elim_results %>%
  filter(Ontology_Branch %in% c("BP", "MF")) %>%
  mutate(
    Truncated_GO_Name = str_remove(GO_Name, ",.*$"),
    Clean_GO_Name = str_remove(Truncated_GO_Name, "\\s+activity$"),
    neg_log_p = -log10(p.adjust),
    Wrapped_GO_Name = str_wrap(Clean_GO_Name, width = 50)
  ) %>%
  # Route terms directly into the four core conceptual pillars
  mutate(
    Facet_Group = case_when(
      # Pillar 1: Initial attack and ring breaking
      str_detect(GO_Name, "(?i)monooxygenase|dioxygenase|hydroxylase|aromatic.*degrad|cleavage") &
        !str_detect(GO_Name, "(?i)glycine|aldehyde") ~ "1. Phase-1 Oxidation & Ring Cleavage",

      # Pillar 2: Neutralizing toxic downstream intermediates
      str_detect(GO_Name, "(?i)aldehyde|alcohol.*dehydrogenase|detoxification.*aldehyde") ~ "2. Phase-2 Intermediate Cleanup",

      # Pillar 3: Siphoning waste nitrogen safely
      str_detect(GO_Name, "(?i)nitrogen.*detox|ammonia|urea|glutamate.*dehydrogenase") ~ "3. Nitrogen Waste Management",

      # Pillar 4: Harvesting electrons and folate carbon recycling
      str_detect(GO_Name, "(?i)glycine.*cleavage|decarboxylation.*glycine|folate|tetrahydrofolate|one-carbon|formate|serine.*hydroxymethyl") ~ "4. 1-Carbon Energy Shunts",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  # Keep only the rows that successfully snapped into our 4-pillar network
  filter(!is.na(Facet_Group))

# Safeguard horizontal column integrity against dropout
all_possible_clusters <- unique(compiled_elim_results$Analysis_Group)

# 2. CREATE MATRIX FOR INTER-BLOCK CLUSTERING
matrix_faceted <- fig6_faceted_data %>%
  select(Wrapped_GO_Name, Analysis_Group, neg_log_p) %>%
  distinct(Wrapped_GO_Name, Analysis_Group, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  tidyr::complete(Wrapped_GO_Name, Analysis_Group = all_possible_clusters, fill = list(neg_log_p = 0)) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = Analysis_Group, values_from = neg_log_p, values_fill = 0) %>%
  tibble::column_to_rownames("Wrapped_GO_Name")

if (nrow(matrix_faceted) > 1) {
  # --- MATHEMATICAL AXIS 1: AUTOMATE VERTICAL ROWS (GO TERMS) ---
  row_dist_fac <- dist(matrix_faceted, method = "euclidean")
  row_hc_fac <- hclust(row_dist_fac, method = "complete")
  ordered_rows_fac <- rownames(matrix_faceted)[row_hc_fac$order]

  # --- MATHEMATICAL AXIS 2: AUTOMATE HORIZONTAL COLUMNS (SCATTERPLOT CLUSTERS) ---
  col_dist_fac <- dist(t(matrix_faceted), method = "euclidean")
  col_hc_fac <- hclust(col_dist_fac, method = "complete")
  ordered_columns_fac <- colnames(matrix_faceted)[col_hc_fac$order]

  # 3. INTERLOCK BOTH AXES AS STRICT COMPLETED FACTORS
  fig6_faceted_data$Wrapped_GO_Name <- factor(fig6_faceted_data$Wrapped_GO_Name, levels = ordered_rows_fac)
  fig6_faceted_data$Analysis_Group <- factor(fig6_faceted_data$Analysis_Group, levels = ordered_columns_fac)

  # 4. ENFORCE TOTAL CROSS-GRID PLOTTING INTEGRITY
  grid_faceted <- expand_grid(
    Analysis_Group = factor(ordered_columns_fac, levels = ordered_columns_fac),
    Wrapped_GO_Name = factor(ordered_rows_fac, levels = ordered_rows_fac)
  ) %>%
    left_join(distinct(fig6_faceted_data, Wrapped_GO_Name, Facet_Group), by = "Wrapped_GO_Name") %>%
    left_join(fig6_faceted_data, by = c("Analysis_Group", "Wrapped_GO_Name", "Facet_Group")) %>%
    mutate(
      neg_log_p = replace_na(neg_log_p, 0),
      Wrapped_Facet = str_wrap(Facet_Group, width = 18)
    )

  # Calculate dynamic panel safety height (0.32 inch row packing)
  h6_faceted <- max(5.5, (length(unique(grid_faceted$Wrapped_GO_Name)) * 0.32) + 2)

  # 5. GENERATE THE 4-PILLAR FACETED HEATMAP
```

```{r}
# ==============================================================================
# FACETED DETOXIFICATION & METABOLIC SHUNT INFRASTRUCTURE

message("Compiling expanded, 4-panel faceted detoxification heatmap...")

# 1. EXPANDED SEARCH & CORE HEURISTIC ROUTING
fig6_faceted_data <- compiled_elim_results %>%
  filter(Ontology_Branch %in% c("BP", "MF")) %>%
  mutate(
    Truncated_GO_Name = str_remove(GO_Name, ",.*$"),
    Clean_GO_Name = str_remove(Truncated_GO_Name, "\\s+activity$"),
    neg_log_p = -log10(p.adjust),
    Wrapped_GO_Name = str_wrap(Clean_GO_Name, width = 50)
  ) %>%
  # Route terms directly into the four core conceptual pillars
  mutate(
    Facet_Group = case_when(
      # Pillar 1: Initial attack and ring breaking
      str_detect(GO_Name, "(?i)monooxygenase|dioxygenase|hydroxylase|aromatic.*degrad|cleavage") &
        !str_detect(GO_Name, "(?i)glycine|aldehyde") ~ "1. Phase-1 Oxidation & Ring Cleavage",

      # Pillar 2: Neutralizing toxic downstream intermediates
      str_detect(GO_Name, "(?i)aldehyde|alcohol.*dehydrogenase|detoxification.*aldehyde") ~ "2. Phase-2 Intermediate Cleanup",

      # Pillar 3: Siphoning waste nitrogen safely
      str_detect(GO_Name, "(?i)nitrogen.*detox|ammonia|urea|glutamate.*dehydrogenase") ~ "3. Nitrogen Waste Management",

      # Pillar 4: Harvesting electrons and folate carbon recycling
      str_detect(GO_Name, "(?i)glycine.*cleavage|decarboxylation.*glycine|folate|tetrahydrofolate|one-carbon|formate|serine.*hydroxymethyl") ~ "4. 1-Carbon Energy Shunts",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  # Keep only the rows that successfully snapped into our 4-pillar network
  filter(!is.na(Facet_Group))

# Safeguard horizontal column integrity against dropout
all_possible_clusters <- unique(compiled_elim_results$Analysis_Group)

# 2. CREATE MATRIX FOR INTER-BLOCK CLUSTERING
matrix_faceted <- fig6_faceted_data %>%
  select(Wrapped_GO_Name, Analysis_Group, neg_log_p) %>%
  distinct(Wrapped_GO_Name, Analysis_Group, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  tidyr::complete(Wrapped_GO_Name, Analysis_Group = all_possible_clusters, fill = list(neg_log_p = 0)) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = Analysis_Group, values_from = neg_log_p, values_fill = 0) %>%
  tibble::column_to_rownames("Wrapped_GO_Name")

if (nrow(matrix_faceted) > 1) {
  # --- MATHEMATICAL AXIS 1: AUTOMATE VERTICAL ROWS (GO TERMS) ---
  row_dist_fac <- dist(matrix_faceted, method = "euclidean")
  row_hc_fac <- hclust(row_dist_fac, method = "complete")
  ordered_rows_fac <- rownames(matrix_faceted)[row_hc_fac$order]

  # --- MATHEMATICAL AXIS 2: AUTOMATE HORIZONTAL COLUMNS (SCATTERPLOT CLUSTERS) ---
  col_dist_fac <- dist(t(matrix_faceted), method = "euclidean")
  col_hc_fac <- hclust(col_dist_fac, method = "complete")
  ordered_columns_fac <- colnames(matrix_faceted)[col_hc_fac$order]

  # 3. INTERLOCK BOTH AXES AS STRICT COMPLETED FACTORS
  fig6_faceted_data$Wrapped_GO_Name <- factor(fig6_faceted_data$Wrapped_GO_Name, levels = ordered_rows_fac)
  fig6_faceted_data$Analysis_Group <- factor(fig6_faceted_data$Analysis_Group, levels = ordered_columns_fac)

  # 4. ENFORCE TOTAL CROSS-GRID PLOTTING INTEGRITY
  grid_faceted <- expand_grid(
    Analysis_Group = factor(ordered_columns_fac, levels = ordered_columns_fac),
    Wrapped_GO_Name = factor(ordered_rows_fac, levels = ordered_rows_fac)
  ) %>%
    left_join(distinct(fig6_faceted_data, Wrapped_GO_Name, Facet_Group), by = "Wrapped_GO_Name") %>%
    left_join(fig6_faceted_data, by = c("Analysis_Group", "Wrapped_GO_Name", "Facet_Group")) %>%
    mutate(
      neg_log_p = replace_na(neg_log_p, 0),
      Wrapped_Facet = str_wrap(Facet_Group, width = 18)
    )

  # Calculate dynamic panel safety height (0.32 inch row packing)
  h6_faceted <- max(5.5, (length(unique(grid_faceted$Wrapped_GO_Name)) * 0.32) + 2)

  # 5. GENERATE THE 4-PILLAR FACETED HEATMAP
  plot_fig6_faceted <- ggplot(grid_faceted, aes(x = Analysis_Group, y = Wrapped_GO_Name)) +
    geom_tile(aes(fill = neg_log_p), color = "white", lwd = 0.3) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "rocket", direction = -1, name = "-log10(p)") +

    # Slice rows dynamically by functional pillar, letting each panel handle its own height sizing
    facet_grid(Wrapped_Facet ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, face = "bold"),
      axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8.5, lineheight = 0.85, face = "bold"),
      panel.grid = element_blank(),
      strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 90, face = "bold", size = 9, lineheight = 0.95, vjust = 0.5),
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "gray95", color = "gray85", linewidth = 0.5),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
      panel.spacing.y = unit(0.7, "lines")
    ) +
    labs(
      title = "Coordinated Detoxification & Metabolic Shunt Cascades",
      subtitle = "4-Pillar View: Upstream ring breakdown, intermediate clearance, waste tracking, and energy recovery",
```

```{r}
message("Compiling tightly clustered Figure 4...")

      str_detect(GO_Name, "(?i)fatty acid beta-oxidation|fatty acid metabolic|fatty acid biosyn|fatty acid syn|acyl-coa") &
        !str_detect(GO_Name, "(?i)targeting|localization|tRNA|translation|protein acylation|transporter|binding|hydrolase") ~ "1. Fatty Acid Core Lifecycle",

      # Panel 2: Tightly restricted lipid-specific transporters
      str_detect(GO_Name, "(?i)lipid.*transporter|transmembrane.*lipid") ~ "2. Lipid Translocation Machinery",

      # Panel 3: Tightly restricted cell wall architecture
      str_detect(GO_Name, "(?i)cell wall organization") ~ "3. Outer Envelope Armor",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  # Drop the unassigned broad transport strings and enzymatic noise
  filter(!is.na(Facet_Group))

# 2. LOCALIZED CLUSTERING ENGINE: Forcing terms into tight adjacent rows
y_axis_sorter <- fig4_consolidated %>%
  distinct(Wrapped_GO_Name, GO_Name, Facet_Group) %>%
  mutate(
    # Numeric ranking to physically stack the lifecycle components together
    Micro_Cluster = case_when(
      Facet_Group == "1. Fatty Acid Core Lifecycle" & str_detect(GO_Name, "(?i)beta-oxidation") ~ 1.1,
      Facet_Group == "1. Fatty Acid Core Lifecycle" & str_detect(GO_Name, "(?i)acyl-coa") ~ 1.2,
      Facet_Group == "1. Fatty Acid Core Lifecycle" & str_detect(GO_Name, "(?i)biosynthetic|synth") ~ 1.3,
      TRUE ~ 1.4
    )
  ) %>%
  # Sort by broad facet panel first, then by our strict biological micro-clusters
  arrange(Facet_Group, Micro_Cluster, GO_Name)

# Force the text labels into a strict factor order based on this localized cluster sort
fig4_consolidated$Wrapped_GO_Name <- factor(
  fig4_consolidated$Wrapped_GO_Name,
  levels = unique(y_axis_sorter$Wrapped_GO_Name)
)

# 3. ENFORCE MATRIX GRID INTEGRITY

  Analysis_Group = unique(compiled_elim_results$Analysis_Group),
  Wrapped_GO_Name = unique(fig4_consolidated$Wrapped_GO_Name)
) %>%
  left_join(distinct(fig4_consolidated, Wrapped_GO_Name, Facet_Group), by = "Wrapped_GO_Name") %>%
  left_join(fig4_consolidated, by = c("Analysis_Group", "Wrapped_GO_Name", "Facet_Group")) %>%

  )

  ) +
  labs(
```
